items.question: Why do you think inference-time compute is important for achieving general-domain, long-horizon reliability?
items.object: Inference-time compute for general-domain, long-horizon reliability
items.answer: The thing that remains to be solved is general domain long-horizon reliability, and I think you need inference-time compute, test-time compute for that. When you try to prove a new theorem in math, or when you're writing a large software program, or when you're writing an essay of reasonable complexity, you usually wouldn't write token by token. You'd want to think quite hard about some of those tokens, and finding ways to spend not 1x or 2x or 10x but a million x the resources on that token in a productive way, I think, is really important. That is probably the last big problem.

items.question: Why did pursuing AI feel like the right choice to you at age 14?
items.object: AI as a meaningful pursuit
items.answer: I think I just had my midlife crisis when I was 14. I was just looking for something meaningful to do, spent about a year looking at physics, math, bio, medicine, just anything really that seemed valuable to the world. At some point, I bumped into simply the idea of AI. It hadn't occurred to me until then. If you could just build a system, a computer system, that could do all this other stuff for me, great, I don't have to decide. So it felt like my decision paralysis was sort of resolved. It was this weird moment where I could just see the next 30 years of my life unfold in front of me, and I was like, okay, this is clearly what's going to happen. I have to do this. It was quite nice. I like predictability, so it was great to know what the world will look like.

items.question: What made pursuing AGI feel like an executable research agenda to you?
items.object: AGI as an executable research agenda combining language models and reinforcement learning
items.answer: I have been running around with this AGI to-do list, which is somewhat of a meme internally because we just go through it and try to fix all these problems. I've been running around with a version of this. In 2017 or so, when I was still in high school, some conference invited me to present my AGI to-do list. It was wrong at the time. I was also sure it was wrong. I don't like blue-sky research in the sense of just staring at a wall and trying to figure out what the right question is. I really like to have the question and then look for the right answer when starting an intense project, because you need to know which direction you run in to really plan for it. Many things seemed clear, but it seemed completely unclear how to make these models reason in the general domain. That became more clear with language models, especially code models. When I saw some of these early results in the space, I was like, “Okay, I know all this stuff from the RL world. I have a bunch of other thoughts. This seems great. We should just take LMs and make them do the RL stuff.” Very simple proposal, but I think that's where it makes a lot of sense. RL has been doing this for 10 years; it works in restricted domains. It seemed pursuable. items.question: How do you think committing to building AI at fourteen shaped your development as a researcher?
items.object: Committing early to a career building AI
items.answer: I can only really speak for the sort of profile of goals and person I am. I think I was lucky in the sense that I knew very, very early, at 14, exactly what I wanted to do with my life. I had no doubt at all, and uncertainty can be paralyzing to a lot of people. I also had a very clear sense that I did not at all have a plan B. There was no other path in life that I would have been even remotely above the neutral line on. It had to be build AI; everything else is completely irrelevant. I understand that for many people, a paying job at Google is a great achievement. If it's on AI, it's fine, but you get what I mean. I just knew there was nothing else I could do and be fulfilled in life and look back when I'm 90 and be happy. In a way, burning the boats very, very early gives you the opportunity to do things you'd otherwise do 10 years later. I sucked at the beginning. It took me two months to understand the first paper I tried to understand. I was terrible at programming for a long time. But when you're a teenager, you're a decent researcher; you don't have to be great. That gets you things like a great mentor who then bashes you for a year, which was very helpful. Then you get better and you're still young, so your brain shapes more easily, maybe. I feel like I benefited a lot from being early.

items.question: How do you think aspiring AI researchers should approach getting the help they need to reach their end goal?
items.object: Pursuing research goals directly and seeking expert mentorship
items.answer: I'd say just go for the end goal immediately. Doing anything like, “Oh, I'm going to do a PhD because I need a PhD to get a—” that's all bullshit. You don't. The other thing is, writing five-page emails to people actually works. I get a lot of these two-paragraph messages now, and I'm grateful I get emails, but I understand why people think this stuff doesn't work. It certainly does when you're like, “Here is how I'm going to beat your algorithm. Please help me.” Five pages, at least in my experience, every single time anyone I wanted help from in this way was very helpful. Be proactive in seeking the best people in the world to, in a time-efficient manner, distill their brain into yours, and show them that you can make use of that. If you tell someone who's very good, effectively, “I'm going to make good use of this. If you want to coach someone, I would love to be that person,” they'll usually do it. items.question: Why do you place so much value on reading research papers broadly?
items.object: Reading research papers broadly
items.answer: Fundamentally, you need to understand the domain you work in. It's also really good to just read everything. I used to read, I don't know, every paper I could, every paper I would see, basically. Eventually you get so fast at it that it's feasible, and you build a database in your head: this is similar to this thing. Bill Gates has this interview, like, “Oh yeah, if you learned enough things, they're all similar to each other, so it's not linear; it gets easier.” At that point I was like, I should read every paper. Thanks for the advice, Bill. Obviously it was through a video; I never met him. I just started reading every paper, and that's really, really helpful because a lot of the best ideas that we had that work really well now at Magic were enabled by random things. It would never work without this random thing that I would have had to come up with in tandem. Because I have this database in my head, I can go, “Oh yeah, this.” So often one good idea is enabled by three other ideas that others have come up with, and it's always this composition of stuff. Having a large database is really helpful.

items.question: How did the research setback you faced with your high-school mentor Johannes shape your attitude toward persistence?
items.object: Persisting through a research setback with his mentor Johannes
items.answer: It can take ages to do good work. There was one moment with Johannes, the DeepMind research scientist who mentored me for a year in high school, where we had a version of the algorithm that wasn't very good. It was all right, and we were thinking, “Should we publish this?” We were both not really happy about it, and he was close to giving up on me. “Maybe this is just not going to work. I wouldn't want to publish this.” I was like, “Dude, [expletive] you, I'm just going to get this done,” and then we got it done a month or two later. I remember going on a walk after this and just being like, “Can I do this? I don't know if I can do this, but there is no other option, so I better get it done.” Then I went back home and started programming again. I was still sad that day, but the next day was fine again. Just keep going. I think that was a pretty formative experience, because I actually wasn't sure if I could do it, and then we did it super soon after. I haven't felt that insane level of doubt and pressure since then, which has enabled me. I think it's actually beneficial. You have to be realistic.

items.question: How do you think synthesis and conceptual leaps fit together in producing the best AI research ideas?

items.question: How do you think about competing to build AGI against companies with far more funding and hardware?
items.object: The funding and compute needed to build AGI and compete with larger AI companies
items.answer: The question is how much does it cost to build AGI, not how much money can you raise. If you can build AGI for however much you can raise, having more might help you, but it won't get you there substantially sooner, right? If you have all the right ideas and you can build it with a certain amount of hardware, by definition, if someone had 100 times more hardware, would it be computing that much faster or whatever? It doesn't seem like a material advantage if your estimate for how much compute you need to build AGI is not as high as the revenue these companies can generate or the funding they raise. It is, in fact, much lower. I think that is the case. It's not by any means accessible. It's very damn hard to get that much money, but it's not 100 billion. If I'm wrong, I'm wrong, and it'll be 100 billion, and we will not have 100 billion, and that's it. But if we can get to that point where we have AGI and a couple others have AGI, then the benefit of additional compute there—and you show an ROI—it's a reasonably even playing field in terms of additional revenue. You're going to bring AI to the market; you're going to raise more on it. The starting condition of having this hardware is that you need sufficient hardware, but you don't need more than sufficient. That's a bet, not something you know, but I think it's a bet with a high enough probability of being right that it is reasonable to compete in the space. I think it is reasonable to think that the ROI of having sufficient funding might be better than the ROI of having infinite funding early on.

items.question: What kind of working relationship do you want people to have with an AI coding agent?
items.object: An AI coding agent that feels like a colleague
items.answer: Fundamentally, there are two tiers here—I guess three. One is useless, the next is an assistant that you have to micromanage, and then the next is the thing that manages you, basically, where it's sort of more like a colleague. I think the layer where it's exactly even doesn't really exist, because it's sort of this little thin point once the model is more competent than you are. You are there to give it guidance on what you want to be accomplished and answer clarification questions, but you'll never have to tell it, “Here's a bug.” I'm not saying this is version one of our product, but fundamentally that has to be the goal. items.question: Why do you think Needle in a Haystack can give a misleading impression of a model’s long-context ability?
items.object: Needle in a Haystack as an evaluation of long-context models
items.answer: With Needle in a Haystack, basically what you're testing is, “Find this weird thing, the needle, in this giant pool of not-weird stuff, the haystack.” All you need to be able to do is take a little backpack and walk from the start of the context to the end of the context, find the weird thing, put it in your backpack, and return it. You have to sort of have the implicit prior that this thing is weird, so you're more likely to remember it, which sort of means that you actually don't need to remember the whole context window. You don't need to know all of it. That allows some models, I would say, to look like they're doing long context really well when really it's not working as well.

items.question: Why do you consider Magic’s hash-based evaluation a good general-purpose measure of long-context ability?
items.object: Magic’s hash-based long-context evaluation
items.answer: We decided to go the complete opposite, super hardcore mode, and just replace everything with random noise. There's no semantic information at all because it's just randomly generated letters, basically just hashes. If you did something like Needle in a Haystack in a pool of hashes, you really have to know the whole thing. But then what we do is we also do a hop, so it's not just you find this one thing, but you find this one thing and then you find another thing. Obviously, you can keep that going. Those two dimensions, I think, really are the important quantitative components of context. There are other things you can measure much better in more domain-specific evals, of course. We care a lot about code, so we look a lot at that internally too. From a general-purpose context evaluation perspective, the reason we chose to open source this eval and only this eval is that I think this quantifies exactly what you want to measure when you think about long context. Everything else is domain-specific.
